title: Nearly two-thirds of what the Berlin Airlift flew in was coal, not food

cover.alt: Grainy black-and-white film still of a four-engined transport plane flying low over flat ground, coming in to land.

body: On 24 June 1948 the Soviet Union cut the Western Allies’ railway, road and canal access to West Berlin, but the agreed air corridors stayed open. Allied planes, mostly American and British, flew in about **2.3 million tons** of supplies on 278,228 flights before the airlift ended on 30 September 1949, and nearly two-thirds of it was coal. The city’s food needs stayed at around 1,500 tons a day, but once autumn came, the coal needed to heat it added thousands of tons more to every day’s load.

slides.alt: Grainy black-and-white film: two four-engined transport planes, one after the other, fly low over the camera and descend towards a distant runway.
slides.caption: Rhein-Main air base near Frankfurt, 1948: four-engined airlift transports come in low over the camera, one after another, to land.

slides.heading: West Berlin’s daily airlift target from 20 October 1948
slides.note: 5,620 tons a day in all, including 2 tons of medical supplies.

slides.question: At the height of the airlift, how often did a plane reach West Berlin?
slides.explanation: Every thirty seconds. Planes flew a strict timetable, and from August 1948 each had only one chance to land: a missed approach meant flying back to base.

slides.label: for a twelve-man crew to unload 10 tons of coal from a C-54, a record
slides.text: Berliners did almost all of the unloading and runway repairs themselves, in return for extra rations.

slides.question: Which Berlin airport was built from scratch in under 90 days during the airlift?
slides.explanation: French military engineers and German crews built Tegel, its first runway mostly by hand, working day and night. It later grew into Berlin Tegel Airport.
